edge_cases.scenario: A consumer disputes a charged-off credit card through Experian. The debt is genuinely hers and the reported balance, dates, and status are all accurate; she disputed because she believes the account 'shouldn't be there' after a hardship. The furnisher does a cursory records-only check and verifies within 25 days. She asks whether the furnisher violated the FCRA.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node encodes duties and the reasonable-investigation gloss but omits the threshold element courts require for any § 1681s-2(b) claim: the consumer must show the furnished information was actually inaccurate or materially misleading. Applied as encoded, the checklist's dispositive 'bare records check = inadequate investigation' item would tell a consumer with accurate reporting that the furnisher breached, when in fact her claim fails at the accuracy element regardless of how shoddy the investigation was. This is the single most common way furnisher-dispute claims are dismissed.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer disputes a wrong-balance tradeline through TransUnion; the furnisher parrots its internal records and verifies it, and the error persists for eight months before being corrected. The consumer suffered no denial of credit, no rate increase, and no out-of-pocket loss, and asks what she can recover. Separately, a different consumer asks about a furnisher's failure to investigate a dispute from four years ago.
edge_cases.gap_description: The node covers only duties and (via the practical-enforcement note) the existence of a private right under subsection (b), but encodes nothing about remedies or timing: § 1681o negligent violations require proof of actual damages (emotional-distress or economic), statutory damages of $100–$1,000 are available only for willful violations under § 1681n, and § 1681p imposes a 2-year-from-discovery / 5-year-from-violation limitations period. As encoded, a no-damages consumer would be told she has a viable claim and a time-barred consumer would be told nothing about the bar — materially misleading on the practical question ('what do I get / can I still sue?') that such consumers actually present.

edge_cases.scenario: A consumer signs up with a credit-repair outfit that sends the CRA a third round of boilerplate disputes on the same tradeline with no new information. The CRA deems the dispute frivolous under § 1681i(a)(3), notifies the consumer, and never forwards it to the furnisher. The consumer then wants to sue the furnisher for failing to investigate.
edge_cases.gap_description: The checklist's first dispositive item asks only whether the consumer 'disputed the item directly with a credit bureau,' which the consumer did — but the trigger actually requires that the CRA forwarded the dispute (an ACDV/notice under § 1681i(a)(2)). Where the CRA deems a dispute frivolous or otherwise never forwards it, no furnisher duty arises at all. Given how common template/duplicate disputes are, the checklist as written will lead consumers (and the node's users) to find a breached duty where the trigger never fired; the checklist should ask whether the furnisher actually received CRA notice, not merely whether the consumer filed with a CRA.
